originalTitle: ACLU blasts Trump’s new orders on birthright citizenship, saying they are doomed to fail in court– live
summary: President’s orders come month after supreme court struck down administration’s earlier attempt to place restrictions on birthright citizenship enshrined in US constitution
content: Despite an endorsement from Donald Trump on Thursday, congressman Andy Ogles, a a virulently anti-Muslim Tennessee Republican, seems to be in danger of losing his re-election bid to a primary challenger backed by the state’s governor, Bill Lee. With nearly two-thirds of the votes counted in the party’s primary on Thursday night, Ogles trails Charlie Hatcher, a former state commissioner of agriculture, by more than 5 points, according to a running tally from the Associated Press. “Congressman Andy Ogles is doing a fantastic job representing the incredible people of Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District!” Trump wrote on his social media platform as Tennessee Republicans went to the polls on Thursday. “Andy Ogles my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election. Election Day for the Republican Primary is TODAY. GET OUT AND VOTE FOR ANDY”. An Ogles defeat would be the second loss of a Trump-backed candidate in a Republican primary this week. The executive orders signed on Thursday by Donald Trump, in which he tries, again, to undermine the guarantee of birthright citizenship enshrined in the US constitution reaffirmed by the supreme court just five weeks ago, is part of a quixotic campaign he has waged for more than a decade. At a Republican presidential primary campaign event in Orlando, Florida in November 2015, Trump hinted that he had a plan to end what he called the scourge of “anchor babies”, a derogatory term for children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States as citizens. “You can’t come into the country- you’re illegal, you come down, you sit down, you have your baby, and we take care of the baby for the next 85 years!” Trump said. “Everybody says, ‘Well, you need a constitutional amendment; it’ll take 15 years; it’ll never happen’. You don’t, you don’t. You need a simple act of Congress. You might not even need that.” If elected, Trump promised the crowd at a resort near Disney World, “the anchor baby, birthright citizenship, it’s over, not going to happen.” Three years later, as president, Trump said in a televised interview with Jonathan Swan just before the 2018 midterms that he planned to issue an executive order to instruct federal agencies that children born in the United States to non-citizens were not entitled to US citizenship at birth. “It was always told to me that you needed a constitutional amendment. Guess what? You don’t,” Trump told Swan in an interview excerpt posted online on 30 October 2018. “You can definitely do it with an act of Congress,” Trump added, incorrectly, “but now they’re saying I can do it just with an executive order.” As Swan reported at the time, Trump’s claim that he could undo the birthright citizenship guaranteed by the 14th Amendment to the constitution was a minority view among legal scholars, but was supported by a then-obscure figure: John Eastman, who had argued for decades that the amendment granting citizenship to “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” should be read to exclude the children of people who are not US citizens when their child is born. Eastman later claimed in a 2020 Newsweek op-ed that Kamala Harris was ineligible for the vice-presidency because she had no right to US citizenship at birth, since she was born in Oakland, California in 1964 to non-citizen parents who were, “subject to the jurisdiction” of their native lands of India and Jamaica. In the 2018 interview, Trump called birthright citizenship “ridiculous,” and falsely asserted that the US is “the only country in the world where a person comes in and has a baby, and the baby is essentially a citizen.” In fact, at least 30 nations grant citizenship this way. He also claimed that an executive order was in the process of being drafted. Although that order did not materialize until the start of Trump’s second term, his obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had a clearly political element from the start. After all, Trump’s original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claim that Barack Obama, born to an American mother and a Kenyan father in Honolulu, just two years after Hawaii became a state, might have been born outside the US. Then, after Joe Biden picked Harris as his running mate in 2020, Trump repeatedly refused to confirm that she was eligible for an elected office open only to “a natural born Citizen.” Instead, Trump called the question Eastman raised about Harris’s citizenship at birth in his Newsweek op-ed “very serious” and a potential “problem” for her. He also praised Eastman as “a very highly qualified, very talented lawyer” and called him “brilliant”. Eastman, who went on to devise the fake electors scheme designed to keep Trump in office after he lost the 2020 election, and gave an inflammatory speech before the Capitol riot on January 6 2021, was finally disbarred by the California supreme court in April, based on “clear and convincing evidence that he advanced false claims about the 2020 presidential election to mislead courts, public officials, and the American public.” The American Civil Liberties Union is not impressed by the legal reasoning of Donald Trump’s new executive orders in which he is once again attempting to restrict birthright citizenship, just five weeks after the US supreme court struck a similar order he issued last year. In a statement, the ACLU blasted the president’s attempted end-run around the supreme court decision and predicted that the new orders will not survive a court challenge. “The Supreme Court already decided this issue: Birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution. No additional executive order can change the meaning of the Constitution,” the deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, Cody Wofsy, said. “Any executive order that tries to rewrite birthright citizenship will meet the same fate as the last one”. chineseContent: 尽管周四得到了唐纳德·特朗普的支持，田纳西州共和党议员安迪·奥格尔斯是一位恶毒的反穆斯林共和党人，但他似乎面临连任失败的危险，输给了该州州长比尔·李支持的初选挑战者。据美联社的实时统计，周四晚该党初选已清点近三分之二的选票，奥格尔斯落后前州农业专员查理·哈切尔 (Charlie Hatcher) 超过 5 个百分点。 “国会议员安迪·奥格尔斯（Andy Ogles）代表田纳西州第五国会选区令人难以置信的人民做了出色的工作！”田纳西州共和党人周四前往投票站时，特朗普在其社交媒体平台上写道。 “安迪向我投来了对连任的完全和完全支持。今天是共和党初选的选举日。出去投票给安迪”。奥格尔斯的失败将是特朗普支持的候选人在本周的共和党初选中第二次失利。唐纳德·特朗普周四签署的行政命令再次试图破坏五周前最高法院重申的美国宪法中规定的与生俱来的公民身份保障，这是他十多年来发起的不切实际的竞选活动的一部分。 2015 年 11 月，在佛罗里达州奥兰多举行的共和党总统初选活动上，特朗普暗示，他有一项计划来结束他所谓的“锚婴儿”祸害，“锚婴儿”是对在美国出生的无证移民子女的贬义词。 “你不能进入这个国家——你是非法的，你下来，你坐下来，你生了你的孩子，我们在接下来的 85 年里照顾这个孩子！”特朗普说道。 “每个人都说，‘嗯，你需要宪法修正案；这需要 15 年的时间；这永远不会发生’。你不需要，你会
